My wife had a C-section.

  1. Make sure that you plan your C-section well ahead of time. You will want to meet with the surgeon, and that you're comfortable with him/her. Listen to make sure that your OB is collaborating with your surgeon; otherwise you might end up with two different recovery paths. Reducing the bullshit while you're in postpartum will reduce your stress and make that period less of a total clusterfuck.

  2. They may want to give you Pitocin following the procedure; this is normal, but can have consequences. I'm not a doctor. I've spent time working in hospital and I read quite a lot about biology (proteomics, hormones, medicine, etc.) Take my opinion on this with a grain of salt. Pitocin is very helpful in getting your lady parts back into the positions they enjoyed before your house-guest went all Koolaid Man; but if they want to give you an increased dose, make sure it's necessary. Pitocin is synthetic Oxytocin, which is the hormone that your brain is going to make heavy use if in postpartum bonding. Having too much of the synthetic hormone in your system when you're recovering can cause depression and retard the bonding process. This is something that some healthcare providers won't tell you. I'm not trying to scare you. If you find yourself feeling bummed out and not feeling like your bonding with your daughter, or that you're a shit mother - it's your body drawing confused conclusions. It can and most often does get better on its own with time and support. Try to remember this and you'll do well. I'd probably talk to your doctor about depression if you find yourself having trouble caring for your daughter or if you're having unusually dark thoughts, etc. If you have a public health department where you're living, they should have better details about postpartum depression than I do. This whole spiel serves to underscore the importance of #3.

  3. Get as much support as you can. You mentioned that the father isn't going to be able to be there. I took two weeks off when my son was born and went full dadmode. It was still the hardest thing we've ever done. I did a lot of feeding him, changing him collecting biometric data, etc. If you can have someone around, like an older female relative that's been through it before, can be super helpful for your mental health. If you plan on breast feeding, there are a lot of groups on social networks for that and other things like co-sleeping that can be a great source of strength and a place to rant when you need to.

  4. Stay the fuck away from WebMD and the like. Your daughter's going to cough, or do something else that will concern you. You go to the internet, punch in the symptoms and it'll tell you that she has turbo-cancer. Seriously, when you're staying at home with an infant you can develop compulsions and obsess over their health in unhealthy ways. I'm not saying don't pay attention and make a doctor's appointment or go to the ER if you feel it's appropriate; but don't spend hours on the internet looking for reasons to be upset; the lack of sleep is reason enough. Bundle her up, put her in a stroller and go for a walk. It's way better for your sanity.

  5. Consider breastfeeding. It's really none of my business, but there is a lot of data suggesting that breast feeding provides real benefits to babies born via C-section that are missing out on ingesting bits of the vaginal microbiome during the birth process. It probably sounds unpalatable, but seeding your babies intestinal bacteria is really important to her future immune response. Moreover, it really helps with bonding. A C-section birth may interfere with milk production as your body recovers from the trauma, but even a few millilitres of milk in a feeding makes a difference in the microbiome, provides antibodies against infection and more. When our son was born breastfeeding him was like squeezing blood from a stone. Fast forward to a few months later and now it's like he has his pick of a pair of horns of plenty. Bonus? The boob is our last-line of defense against his tyrant bullshit around bedtime. Five minutes on and he's sound asleep. YMMV.
